The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. It is Paraguay’s largest private investment but local people accuse a forestry giant of ignoring their contamination concerns over its vast plantation

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

items.title: [carbonbrief.org] El Niño-linked fires lift total carbon emissions despite fossil fuel dip
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [36kr.com] EU sues IBM, Atos and Leonardo over border system delays
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The European Union has sued IBM, French IT group Atos and Italian defence contractor Leonardo over repeated delays in developing its Entry/Exit System (EES), an electronic border-check system for the 29-country Schengen area. The EU agency eu-LISA filed the civil case in Estonia in December 2025; the dispute became public on Monday. The agency and the European Commission say the case concerns development delays, not the system’s current operation. The system was initially scheduled to launch in 2022 but was not fully rolled out until 2026. Its introduction caused hours-long airport queues after fingerprint scanners malfunctioned, including when exposed to sweat. Some countries are still acquiring scanners. The system records fingerprints and photographs from non-EU travellers on their first entry to help identify visa overstayers and identity fraud. eu-LISA says the case does not affect operations. Estonia’s Harju County Court has accepted the case, but no hearing has been held or scheduled.

Rising costs: The contract’s value increased from €142 million to €212 million in 2021, and eu-LISA nearly doubled the system’s 2023 budget to €40 million, reallocating funds from other projects (ft.com, biggo.com). Penalty challenge: IBM Belgium and Atos Belgium attributed delays partly to the COVID-19 pandemic when challenging an agency penalty (ft.com, reuters.com). items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Hackers used employee access and wallet authorization to steal $6.34 billion from Binance
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said attackers spent months compromising employee computers, then used stolen credentials and a wallet authorization mechanism to bypass normal transfer controls and steal about $6.34 billion on Oct. 29. The FBI attributed the operation to North Korean-linked hackers; North Korea denied responsibility. Binance traced the intrusion to a June infection through a tampered Homebrew installer, followed in September by a fake recruitment process that led another engineer to run a malicious coding assignment. The malware replaced a legitimate development component and evaded endpoint security. By Oct. 20, attackers were using a compromised computer and an internal AI tool to access two wallet engineers’ systems. On Oct. 29, attackers used a stolen deployment token to run a script and exploit Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization feature. Binance said the wallet’s multiparty-computation design meant no single private key could immediately revoke the authorization, requiring it to develop a special procedure. The exchange said it cleared the delegation at 00:10 UTC on Oct. 30. Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool and commissioned independent cybersecurity experts to review the breach.
